summary: Describes how subnet gateways can use the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) to let hosts on connected subnets communicate without knowing subnets exist. This technique is known as Proxy ARP.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1027 describes Proxy ARP, a way for a gateway to hide subnets from the computers on the network. When one computer asks which hardware address belongs to a computer on another network, the gateway answers for that computer and gives its own address instead. The asking computer then sends the traffic to the gateway, which passes it on, so no computer has to be changed to understand subnets.

subtitle: How a gateway can answer address requests for hosts on another network, so no host has to know subnets exist.

tldr.problem: A large Ethernet often has to be split into subnets, but the hosts on it run more than half a dozen different operating systems, and many of them cannot be changed to understand subnet numbers.
tldr.mechanism: A subnet gateway watches for ARP requests. When a host asks for the address of a host on another physical network, the gateway answers for it and gives its own network address, so the asking host sends that traffic to the gateway, which forwards it by ordinary IP routing.
tldr.outcome: The technique needs no changes to any host and no new routing or ARP cache entries in the gateway, and the memo describes a working 4.3BSD implementation of about 110 lines. The authors note it was left out of the 4.3BSD distribution on purpose, to encourage vendors to implement subnets properly.

today: RFC 1027 has not been obsoleted or updated, and the RFC Editor's index gives it no status category. The memo's own account is that the technique was in wide use and that the implementation was deliberately kept out of the 4.3BSD distribution, because the Berkeley group thought that shipping it would reduce the incentive for vendors to implement subnets properly.

sections.title: Why the Subnets Had to Be Hidden
sections.content:
The Ethernet at the University of Texas at Austin was a large installation connecting over ten buildings, with more than one hundred hosts attached to it. Its size and traffic load ruled out tying it together with repeaters, and splitting it into smaller distinct units by the use of subnets was the attractive alternative.

That is exactly the situation the Internet subnet method of RFC 950 is meant for. The difficulty was that many vendors had not yet implemented subnets, and it was not practical to modify the more than half a dozen different operating systems running on the hosts on the local networks. A method for hiding the existence of subnets from the hosts was therefore highly desirable. Since every local area network supported ARP, an ARP-based method was chosen, commonly known as Proxy ARP or the ARP hack. The memo uses the term subnet to mean the RFC 950 subnet method throughout.
sections.plainLanguage: A campus network had grown too large and too busy to connect with repeaters, so it needed to be split into subnets. But the computers on it ran several operating systems that did not understand subnet numbers, and changing them all was not practical. The answer was to let the gateways hide the subnets instead.

sections.title: The Basic Proxy ARP Method
sections.content:
On a network that supports ARP, a host that broadcasts an ARP request for the network address matching the IP address of another host will get a point-to-point ARP reply from that host. The asking host keeps the mapping in a local cache and uses it for later traffic.

If the two hosts are on different physical networks, the target host never sees the request and cannot answer it. But if a gateway connects the two physical networks, the gateway sees the request. Assuming that subnet numbers correspond to physical networks, the gateway can tell that the request is for a host on a different physical network, so it answers for that host and gives its own network address. The asking host caches that reply and sends later IP packets for the target to the gateway, which forwards them by the usual IP routing mechanisms. The gateway is acting as an agent for the target host, which is where the name Proxy ARP comes from; the memo calls such a device a transparent subnet gateway or ARP subnet gateway.

When the target replies, the same algorithm happens in reverse. The two hosts do not need to be connected to the same gateway, only to gateways from which each network is reachable. All of the subnet handling sits in the gateways, so no change is needed to the normal ARP protocol or to routing on the source and target hosts. From the host's point of view there are no subnets, and its physical networks are simply one large IP network. A host that does have a subnet implementation must still set its network mask to cover only the IP network number, leaving the subnet bits out.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally, the computer that owns an address answers the address request itself. A proxying gateway answers in its place when the address belongs to a host on another network, and gives its own address instead. The asking computer then sends that host's traffic to the gateway, which forwards it in the ordinary way.

sections.title: Routing and Multiple Gateways
sections.content:
When an ARP request arrives, the gateway can decide whether it knows a route to the target host by looking in the ordinary routing table, whose entries are expected to include network numbers with the subnet bits included as specified by the subnet mask. The network mask of the interface on which the request arrived is applied to the target IP address to produce the network part that is looked up. The memo assumes the same network mask applies to every subnet of the same IP network.

One special case matters. In 4.3BSD, and probably elsewhere, a default route can exist, naming an address to forward to when no other route is found. The default route must not be used when checking for a route to the target of an ARP request, because the check would then always succeed, and the host named by the default route is unlikely to know about subnet routing, so packets sent to it will probably be lost. This special case in the routing lookup is the only change needed to the routing mechanism.

If the interface on which the request arrived and the interface through which the route to the target passes are the same, the gateway must not reply: either the target is on the same physical network and should answer for itself, or this gateway is not on the most direct path and another gateway on the same physical network is, and that one should respond. The memo's technique is a restricted subset of RFC 925, which describes a general mechanism for dynamic subnet routing with Proxy ARP and routing caches. Here the subnet routes are static and determined administratively, so the gateways need no new network routing table entries and no new ARP cache entries; only the ARP caches in the hosts grow.

More than one gateway may sit between two physical networks, for reliability or to spread traffic. A requesting host uses the first ARP response it receives, which can even give a rudimentary load balancing service, since of two similar gateways the more lightly loaded one is more likely to reply first. The memo notes that gateway-to-gateway protocols would become necessary in networks with many subnets and gateways, in the same way that they are necessary among IP gateways generally.
sections.plainLanguage: Before answering, the gateway checks its own routing table to see whether it can reach the target. It must not use the default route for this check, because the default route would always match and the host behind it would probably not understand subnets. With more than one gateway, the host simply uses whichever reply arrives first, which can also spread traffic between them.

sections.title: The Checks a Gateway Must Make
sections.content:
Three checks decide whether the gateway answers. If the IP networks of the source and target hosts of an ARP request are different, the gateway should not reply, so that it cannot be used to reach foreign IP networks and thereby bypass security checks provided by IP gateways. If the physical networks of the source and target are the same, the gateway must not reply, because either the target can answer for itself or an answer from this gateway would cause a loop.

A request for a broadcast address must elicit no reply, whatever the source address or physical networks involved. If the gateway replied, it would be inviting the original source to send real traffic to a broadcast address, which could cause the Chernobyl effect, in which every host on the network replies and the network melts down.

Broadcast addresses need care as well. There are two kinds of IP broadcast address: the main IP directed network broadcast, and the subnet broadcast, which also includes the subnet number bits. RFC 922 standardised the use of all ones in the local part, but two conventions were in use before it, all ones and all zeros: 4.2BSD used all zeros and 4.3BSD uses all ones, so four kinds of directed broadcast address were still in use. A transparent subnet gateway must not send an IP broadcast using the subnet broadcast address, such as 128.83.138.255, because hosts on the physical network will not understand such an address as a broadcast address; 4.2BSD hosts treat it as a specific host address and try to forward it, which generates an ARP request for a target that does not exist. The memo describes the observed result, a 4.3BSD gateway running the rwho program broadcasting a packet once a minute and causing every 4.2BSD host on the local network to generate an ARP request at the same time. A subnet gateway in a network with hosts that do not understand subnets must therefore use the IP network directed broadcast address instead, and since many hosts with out-of-date software still expect the old-style all-zeros form, the gateway must send its broadcast addresses in that form, for example 128.83.0.0.
sections.plainLanguage: A gateway answers only when it can genuinely forward the traffic: the target must be on the same IP network but a different physical network. It must stay silent for broadcast addresses and for targets on the same physical network, where an answer would loop the traffic back. It must also send broadcasts in the old all-zeros form, because older hosts treat the newer form as a real host address and flood the network with address requests.

sections.title: The 4.3BSD Implementation
sections.content:
The method described in the memo was first implemented in 4.2BSD on top of retrofitted beta-test 4.3BSD subnet code, and then reimplemented as an add-on to the distributed 4.3BSD sources. Most of the new kernel code sits in the generic Ethernet interface module, netinet/if_ether.c. It consists of eight lines in in_arpinput that check that the facility is enabled on the source interface and that the source and target addresses are on different subnets, then call a new routine, if_subarp, and build the ARP response if all checks succeed. That code is reached only when an ARP request arrives and does nothing when the facility is not enabled on the source interface, so the performance of the gateway is very little degraded.

The routine if_subarp, about sixty lines, ensures that the source and target addresses are on the same IP network and that the target is none of the four kinds of directed broadcast address. It then looks for a path to the target, either a network interface with the desired subnet or the routing tables, and a reply is only sent if the ARP gateway is enabled on that interface and the target and source interfaces differ. In netinet/route.c, about eight lines in the main routing table lookup routine, rtalloc, are modified to recognise the pointer passed by if_subarp as a direction not to use the default route, and the processor priority level around the inner lookup is raised because the routine can now be called from network interface interrupts as well as from the software interrupts that drive IP processing.

Another key change is about fifteen lines added to ip_output in netinet/ip_output.c, which rewrite subnet broadcast addresses in packets originating at the gateway as IP network broadcast addresses, so that hosts without subnet code recognise them. A new routine, in_mainnetof, of about fifteen lines is added to netinet/in.c to return the IP network number without the subnet number from an IP address. Two kernel parameter files gain one line each. In total the memo counts approximately 110 lines of kernel source additions, plus four lines added to the ifconfig command so that the facility can be turned on or off per interface, documented in eleven new lines of manual entry.
sections.plainLanguage: The change to the operating system was small: about 110 lines of kernel code, mostly in the Ethernet driver and the routing lookup. It was left out of the 4.3BSD distribution on purpose, because the Berkeley group thought that including it would reduce the incentive for vendors to implement subnets properly.
